title: Multi-language client graceful-degradation and paged-streaming hybrid spec
creator: Lina Park
description: Purpose: Define a cross-language contract for hybrid paged+streaming APIs and graceful client-side degradation. The goal is to give Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs a consistent developer ergonomics story while allowing the service to fall back to page-based responses, preserve correctness for non-idempotent writes, and provide resumability for long-running streams. This PRD clarifies scope (client surface + acceptance tests + compatibility rules) and enumerates constraints, trade-offs, and required infra changes.
background: We’ve had incidents where streaming endpoints are partially available (regional throttling, transient kernel faults), causing client libraries to either fail hard or behave inconsistently across languages. Some clients implement generator/async-iterator patterns; others return paged lists. Customers building robust UIs and batch workers expect: 1) a predictable fallback path when streaming is unavailable, 2) deterministic cursor semantics for pagination, and 3) minimal memory/CPU footprint in clients during reconnection/resume. This ticket unifies the contract and acceptance criteria.
goals: Define a clear client contract for hybrid responses (stream-first, fallback-to-paged)
Specify retry, idempotency, and backoff expectations for sync/async clients
Standardize resumable stream checkpoints across languages
Provide acceptance test matrix and performance targets for SDK PRs
non_goals: Full server implementation details (server side will implement compatible endpoints separately)
Language-specific advanced ergonomic wrappers beyond the base contract
Changing the public HTTP surface or introducing a new wire protocol
requirements: API surface: SDKs MUST expose both a streaming-first API (async iterator / observable / channel) and a paged fetch API (cursor-based).

Fallback behavior: When a streaming connection fails with retryable transient errors (5xx, 429), SDKs MUST attempt transparent fallback to the paged API for that request and surface a single unified result stream to callers.

Resumability: Streams that are resumable by server (server returns a resume_token) MUST allow SDKs to reconnect using the token and continue from the last acknowledged item. Resume tokens are opaque strings returned in stream metadata or final chunk headers.

Idempotency and non-idempotent safety: For endpoints that mutate state, SDKs MUST not retry non-idempotent requests automatically unless client provides an idempotency_token. Retry policy must be opt-in for unsafe operations.

Retries/backoff: Default retry policy for idempotent read-like endpoints: exponential backoff with full jitter, initial_delay=100ms, max_delay=5s, max_attempts=6. SDKs MUST expose configuration to override these values.
Backpressure: Streaming implementations MUST offer an opt-in pull-based flow control API (e.g., request(n) or buffer limit) to avoid unbounded memory usage in clients.
Interface parity: Core primitives and semantics MUST be present in Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs. Language idioms allowed (async iterator vs channel) but behavior must match in acceptance tests.
Error semantics: Clients MUST surface a consistent set of error classes or codes (StreamUnavailable, ResumeFailed, PaginationCursorInvalid, RateLimited, NonIdempotentRetryForbidden).

Compatibility: Minor SDK releases must be backward compatible for the majority of use-cases; breaking changes require release notes and migration guide. SDKs must support server-side feature negotiation via an SDK-friendly header (x-redwood-features) to detect if resume tokens or hybrid responses are supported.
Telemetry: SDKs MUST emit metrics for fallback occurrences, resume successes/failures, retry counts, and average recovery latency so Console can show feature health per-customer.
Resource limits: Streaming SDKs must default to a soft buffer cap (e.g., 16MB of buffered data) and drop/connect with a clear error if client cannot keep up; buffer cap configurable by client app.

Cancellation and context propagation: All SDK calls MUST accept a context/cancellation mechanism (context.Context in Go, AbortSignal in TS, asyncio.CancelledError-aware coroutine in Python) to allow callers to cancel inflight operations cleanly.
tradeoffs_and_decisions: Unified wire change avoided: We decided not to introduce a new wire protocol; we will implement hybrid responses via existing streaming endpoints augmented with optional resume_token metadata to preserve compatibility.
Server-provided resume tokens: Chosen to keep client logic minimal; tokens opaque avoids coupling to server internals but requires server to manage token lifecycle.
Fallback vs explicit: We opted for transparent fallback to reduce client-side complexity for most customers. Edge-case: apps explicitly requiring streaming-only can opt out via request flag.
Memory vs latency: Default conservative buffer cap favors memory safety for typical customer devices; power-users can increase buffer for throughput-sensitive workloads.
acceptance_criteria: Python/TS/Go SDKs implement streaming-first API plus paged fetch API with matching semantics in the test harness.
Automated cross-language acceptance tests pass: simulated stream failure -> SDK transparently falls back to paged API and yields identical items in same order.
Resumable stream test: server returns resume_token every 10s; SDK can reconnect using token and continue without duplicating or dropping items (zero-loss/at-most-once semantics documented).
Retry policy test: idempotent reads retried per default policy; non-idempotent writes do not auto-retry unless idempotency_token is provided. Tests show configurable overrides work.
Backpressure test: clients can apply pull-based control and do not exceed default buffer cap when consumer is slow; error states documented and surfaced as StreamUnavailable or BufferOverflow.
Telemetry: SDK emits fallback and resume metrics to local logging sink during acceptance tests and Console can ingest sample events (end-to-end test harness).

Documentation: Migration guide, examples for Python (async generator), TypeScript (AsyncIterable & AbortSignal), Go (chan + context.Context), and a short section on choosing idempotency tokens are published in docs repo.
Compatibility: Minor SDK bumps produced during implementation do not change default method names; breaking changes gated behind major release and have a published migration plan.
implementation_notes: Server changes: support optional resume_token in stream metadata and hybrid paged endpoints that accept same query parameters + cursor param.
SDK changes: add a lightweight feature-negotiation header and standardized error classes across languages.
Testing: Build a language-agnostic test harness (Golang harness that drives TS and Python via subprocess) that validates ordering, duplication, and telemetry emission.
Docs: include runnable snippets and cookbook for handling partial stream availability and toggling fallback behavior.
risks: Resume token misuse: tokens must be short-lived; server/operator mistakes could enable duplication or stale resumes.
Library surface divergence: teams might introduce language-specific sugar that drifts semantics; require cross-language reviews for feature parity.
Performance regressions: transparent fallback may add a small additional latency for first recovery; must monitor and tune server to minimize impact.
